items.title: NeuroSeq
items.text: NeuroSeq is a neuronal sequencer: it controls the input to a neural network and reads out its output, whether the network is simulated, biological or neuromorphic. The same protocol and analysis run on all three. Source: github.com/neuroseq/neuroseq.

items.title: Concept
items.text:
For any network, NeuroSeq splits the input into a controlled part (set by you) and an uncontrolled part, and the output into an observed part (read out) and an unobserved part. An experiment is a loop:

  1. Design an input array (one row per neuron).
  2. Deliver it to a network.
  3. Read out the response and match it to the same neuron IDs.
  4. Analyse, and optionally choose the next input from the result.

Because each step is substrate independent, a protocol can be developed in simulation and then run unchanged on a microscope or a neuromorphic chip.

items.title: Long path error during install
items.text: pip install fails with OSError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory on a very long path and the hint "this system does not have Windows Long Path support enabled". Fix: in the Registry Editor set LongPathsEnabled under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem to 1 (Microsoft instructions).

items.title: GPU option greyed out in cell segmentation
items.text:
Cellpose and Suite2p use the GPU only if PyTorch has CUDA (NVIDIA) or MPS (Apple Silicon). PyPI's default torch on Windows is CPU-only. Check:

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"

+cpu or False means CPU-only. On a machine with a supported GPU, install a GPU build and relaunch:

uv pip install --torch-backend=auto torch
# without uv (e.g. Conda):
pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

Intel integrated graphics are not supported: segment on a GPU machine and import its _seg.npy. See Imaging data.

items.title: Hodgkin-Huxley Neuron
items.text:
Models a whole-cell patch clamp recording of one neuron without synaptic input (e.g. under synaptic blockers). Input arrays:

  • I_external (pA, positive or negative): 100 ms ramps to ~300 and ~600 pA, then 100 ms steps of 200, 400 and 600 pA.
  • Exc_stimulation, Inh_stimulation (fraction of the maximum opsin conductance): two 100 ms ramps (to ~50% and ~100%) and steps of 25, 50 and 100%.

Opsins are ideal conductances with instant on/off: \(E_{exc} = 0\) mV, \(E_{inh} = -80\) mV, \(g_{exc} = g_{inh} = 0.1\ mS\,cm^{-2}\). There is no noise input. Raising the neuron count adds independent copies. Setting the Na and K conductances to zero models a non-neuronal cell.

items.title: Analysis and plugins
items.text: Analyses run on a selection in any trace, spike or data widget, so they work the same on simulated and recorded data.

items.title: Run an analysis
items.text:
1. Drag to select a neuron × time region.
  2. Right-click it and choose an analysis.

Built-in: Histogram, Histogram 2D, Spike count per neuron, Pearson correlation. Installed plugins are listed below them.

Open analysis in a new window (checkbox at the top of the menu, on by default) opens each result in its own window. Unticked, results go to the Custom Analysis panel (View → Show Custom Analysis), where you can select again and run a follow-up analysis.

items.title: Bundled plugins
items.text:
Plugin Purpose Mean activity / Advanced: Mean activity Mean trace (or spike activity) of the selection; the advanced one has controls. EPSP amplitudes Detects EPSPs and plots their amplitudes (also used by the STDP routines). Estimate membrane parameters Passive membrane parameters from voltage and injected current. Replay MSE (cycle vs reference) MSE and correlation of replay cycles against the first selected cycle. ELiSe target MSE / ELiSe learning curves ELiSe model metrics.

For the ELISE Sequence Learning Network example, the input editor toolbar also shows Analyse ELiSe Replay (target MSE) (replay MSE and correlation of firing_rate_r against the teaching pattern from opsin_exc, saved as .csv) and Run ELiSe Protocol (learning curves). They are enabled once their inputs exist.

items.title: Plugin folders
items.text:
Plugins are discovered from:

  • src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins/ (bundled), and
  • a per-user folder: <user data dir>/neuroseq/analysis_plugins (e.g. ~/.local/share/neuroseq/analysis_plugins on Linux), or the folder in NEUROSEQ_USER_PLUGIN_DIR. The chat assistant writes plugins here after you confirm them.

Every *.py not starting with _ is a plugin. A user plugin whose file name or PLUGIN_ID matches a bundled one is skipped with a warning. New or edited plugins appear the next time the menu opens, without a restart.

items.title: Write a plugin
items.text:
A plugin module defines:

  • PLUGIN_ID: stable internal identifier (used in logs),
  • PLUGIN_NAME: menu label,
  • PLUGIN_ICON: optional QtAwesome icon (e.g. mdi6.chart-line),
  • render_analysis(widget, data, neuron_slice, time_slice): draws the result.

Details: Developer Guide: Analysis plugins.

items.title: Simulations vs. experiments
items.text:
A project holds input arrays, one Brian2 model, and data groups (experiments) from simulation runs and recordings, plus an optional Cellpose segmentation. The same input array drives a simulation and documents what was delivered to a sample, so simulated and recorded responses can be compared directly.

Simulate → Run Simulation and Experiment → Run External Input Function each add a new data group.

items.title: Import from another project
items.text:
File → Import from Project loads parts of another .nseq file. NeuroSeq offers to save the current project first, then asks what to take:

Option Effect Input Arrays Replaces the current input arrays. Model Replaces the model. Simulation data The stored simulation state (only together with Model). Experimental Data Replaces the current data groups.

Chosen parts replace, not merge with, the current ones, and the undo history is cleared. Experimental Data brings the other project's Cellpose segmentation with it, so the data's cell IDs keep matching; if that project has none, the current segmentation stays.

items.title: Compare simulated and recorded data
items.text:
1. Run a simulation.
  2. Import recordings: imaging data or patch-clamp data. Map recorded cells to the model's neuron IDs with the Cellpose ID mapping.
  3. Show one dataset in Neuron data (Traces panel) and the other in All data (Data panel, View → Show Data). Both share the time axis of the input arrays.
  4. Select a region and run the same analysis on each.

Use File → Manage Data to inspect, rename, describe or delete data groups and data sets (see Experiments).

items.title: Analysis plugins
items.text: An analysis plugin adds an entry to the right-click analysis menu of the trace and spike views without changing core code. Using plugins is described in Analysis.

items.title: Writing a plugin
items.text:
A plugin is one .py file (names starting with _ are ignored) that defines render_analysis:

from neuroseq.data import TraceData

PLUGIN_ID = "mean_activity"  # stable, machine-oriented; default: file name
PLUGIN_NAME = "Mean activity"  # menu label; default: file name
PLUGIN_ICON = "mdi6.chart-timeline-variant"  # qtawesome name; default: mdi6.puzzle


def render_analysis(widget, data, neuron_slice, time_slice) -> None:
    ax = widget.subplot  # Matplotlib axes
    if isinstance(data, TraceData):
        ax.plot(widget.traces.mean(axis=0))  # selection already sliced

widget is the CustomAnalysisWidget; useful attributes are subplot, traces or spike_times_ms (the selected region), dt_ms, neuron_slice and time_slice. The menu lists every plugin for every data type, so check data (TraceData, SpikeData, SynapseData) and show a message for unsupported types. Exceptions are caught, logged with the plugin id and shown in the plot.

Examples in src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins/: mean_activity.py (basic) and advanced_mean_activity.py (adds a control bar to the analysis window; guard against adding duplicate controls when the plugin runs again in the same window).

items.title: Where plugins are found
items.text:
Folder Use src/neuroseq/resources/analysis_plugins/ Built-in plugins user_plugins_directory() Per-user plugins, e.g. written by the chat assistant; override with NEUROSEQ_USER_PLUGIN_DIR

User plugins never shadow a built-in file name or PLUGIN_ID. The folders are rescanned each time the menu opens.

items.title: Internals
items.text:
• analysis_plugins.py: discover_analysis_plugins() loads files into AnalysisPlugin(id, label, icon, render) objects.
  • visualization/timeseries_widget.py: builds the menu and emits custom_analysis_requested with a CustomAnalysisType or an AnalysisPlugin.
  • visualization/custom_analysis_widget.py: runs built-in analyses and plugin render callbacks.

Keep plugins thin. Supporting code belongs in a regular package (for ELiSe, src/neuroseq/elise_support/); core code must never import from the plugin folder, which is excluded from coverage.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: NeuroSeq is a neuronal sequencer: one input and readout interface for digital, biological and neuromorphic networks. Contributions are welcome.

items.title: Plugins first, core by discussion
items.text:
Extend NeuroSeq without touching the core whenever possible:

Extension Mechanism Network backend or substrate Custom simulator file Analysis pipeline Analysis plugin file Input protocol Script in the embedded console that writes an input array

There is no plugin interface for closed-loop routines yet; they live in stimulation/dynamic_input/. Changes to core code (anything under src/neuroseq/) need prior discussion with the core developers, in an issue or draft pull request.

items.title: Workflow
items.text:
1. Fork, clone and install in editable mode.
  2. Create a feature branch.
  3. Make the change and add tests, including a scientific validation test when it affects results.
  4. Run uv run pytest and prek run -a.
  5. Open a pull request that explains the user-visible change, links the issue, lists the commands you ran and includes screenshots for UI changes.

Use short, imperative commit subjects. Do not commit generated files (.coverage, coverage.xml, caches, .venv/). If you use AI tools, follow Responsible use of AI.

items.title: Code organisation
items.text:
CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md at the repository root are the authoritative description of the architecture and grouping rules. In short:

  • Group code by workflow (importers/, export/, device_control/, stimulation/, visualization/), not by kind of file.
  • Keep Qt-free logic in its own module; put widget/project coordination in a controller.
  • Change project data only through Project methods so undo history stays consistent.
  • Run long tasks through background_jobs.BackgroundJob.
  • Use qtpy, not PyQt6/PySide6, directly.

items.title: Project workspaces
items.text:
gui.py is the tab shell. Each tab holds a ProjectWorkspace (project_workspace.py) that owns its widgets, controllers, console namespace, undo history and background jobs; Gui.active_workspace is the current tab. Switching tabs does not copy state; playback pauses but jobs keep running and report to their own workspace. GUI state is not saved in .nseq files.

Device connections are shared application resources (workspace_devices.py). SysCon2 replies and ScanImage acquisition results are routed to the requesting workspace; only the active one gets live ScanImage frames. Closing a tab stops its jobs without disconnecting other tabs. Tests: tests/test_project_workspaces.py.

items.title: Custom simulators
items.text: Any network (a simulator, a neuromorphic chip, a remote rig) can act as a NeuroSeq backend: it receives the input arrays and returns an Experiment. Write it as a standalone Python file so it needs no core changes. Using one from the GUI is described in Run external simulators.

items.title: The simulate contract
items.text:
from neuroseq.data import Experiment


def simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=None, progress=None) -> Experiment:
    ...
  • stims_dict: {name: {"array": ndarray (time × neurons), "dt": seconds}}.
  • simulation_time: seconds to simulate in this call.
  • params: flat {name: value} of the project's external_simulate_params.
  • progress (optional keyword): call progress(fraction) with a value in [0, 1] to drive the progress bar. It raises when the user cancels; let that propagate. Omit the keyword if you do not report progress.
  • Return an Experiment with TraceData, SpikeData and/or SynapseData (neuroseq.data) for this chunk only. The GUI offers to import it as a new experiment or append it to an existing one.

external_simulation_example/simulate.py is a commented, file-based example. Project.load_NN() (alias load_external_simulator()) loads either a file path (via runpy, which must define simulate) or neuroseq:<module> for a module in src/neuroseq/example_models/.

items.title: Stateful backends with NN
items.text:
For backends with parameters and state that persists between runs, subclass NN from neuroseq.example_models.NN. It stores the editable parameter schema and cumulative time; the subclass owns the runtime objects.

Member Role __init__(schema) Copies the schema and initialises flat values and time default_params_schema() Schema for the GUI parameter editor flat_default_params() {name: default} from the schema update_params(params) Merges overrides; calls reset() if anything changed simulated_time_seconds Time simulated so far (self._simulated_time_s) reset() Subclass: clear runtime state simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params, progress) Subclass: run one chunk and return an Experiment migrate_project(project) (optional) Upgrades legacy input formats after an archive loads

The defaults raise NotImplementedError (no abc). Keep schema keys and value types simple: the parameter editor reads them. Stateful backends should continue from the previous state and use _simulated_time_s to align time.

For neuroseq:<module>, NeuroSeq takes the simulator from get_simulator(), else NN(), else the module-level simulate. The reference implementation is src/neuroseq/example_models/elise.py.

from neuroseq.data import Experiment
from neuroseq.example_models.NN import NN

DEFAULT_PARAMS = {
    "gain": {"value": 1.0, "default": 1.0, "type": "float",
             "group": "General", "description": "Input gain."},
}


class MyBackend(NN):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(DEFAULT_PARAMS)
        self._runtime = None

    def reset(self) -> None:
        self._runtime = None
        self._simulated_time_s = 0.0

    def simulate(self, stims_dict, simulation_time, params=None, progress=None) -> Experiment:
        self.update_params(params)
        # build or reuse self._runtime, run, update self._simulated_time_s
        raise NotImplementedError


_SIMULATOR = MyBackend()


def get_simulator() -> MyBackend:
    return _SIMULATOR


def simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=None, progress=None) -> Experiment:
    return _SIMULATOR.simulate(stims_dict, simulation_time, params=params, progress=progress)

To ship a backend with an example project, add a factory under src/neuroseq/example_projects/networks/ with @register_example_project and import it in example_projects/__init__.py (see elise_project.py). Bundling a backend this way is a core change; discuss it first (see Contributing).

items.title: Desktop shortcut
items.text: These steps create a desktop shortcut on Windows.

items.title: Installed release
items.text:
Point a shortcut at the installed executable; no terminal or activation is needed.

  1. In the environment where NeuroSeq is installed, print the executable path:
python -c "import sysconfig; from pathlib import Path; print(Path(sysconfig.get_path('scripts')) / 'neuroseq.exe')"

In Conda, use conda run instead so Conda sets up library paths. Find conda.exe with python -c "import os; print(os.environ['CONDA_EXE'])".

  1. Right-click the desktop, choose New > Shortcut, and enter the location in double quotes, for example:
"C:\Users\YourName\neuroseq-env\Scripts\neuroseq.exe"
"C:\Users\YourName\anaconda3\Scripts\conda.exe" run --no-capture-output -n neuroseq neuroseq
  1. Name it NeuroSeq and click Finish.

Recreate the shortcut if you move the environment. Update with python -m pip install --upgrade neuroseq in that environment.

items.title: Development version
items.text:
This shortcut updates a git clone from main and starts it with uv run, so lab machines always run the current code.

  1. Install Git for Windows and uv (pip install uv in a Conda environment also works). Check git --version and uv --version in a new prompt.
  2. Clone over HTTPS (no login needed for updates):
cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
git clone https://github.com/neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq
  1. Create the shortcut from inside the clone (from the Anaconda Prompt with the right environment active if uv came from Conda):
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\install_shortcut.ps1

It also removes an older shortcut to a pip-installed neuroseq.exe unless you pass -KeepOld. Rerun it after moving the clone or uv.

  1. Run uv sync once in the prompt to watch the first, multi-GB install (PyTorch with CUDA). Afterwards, double-click NeuroSeq. After an update that changes dependencies, the shortcut installs them silently; wait for it.

On each start, the shortcut fast-forwards the clone from GitHub, then runs uv run neuroseq. It skips the update (and shows a notice) when the clone is not on main, has changes to tracked files, has unpushed commits, or GitHub is unreachable. It never switches branches; run git switch main yourself.

Logs of the last start are in %LOCALAPPDATA%\neuroseq: launcher.log (update steps, started commit), neuroseq.out.log and neuroseq.err.log (the end of the error log is shown if NeuroSeq fails). To start without updating, for example during an experiment:

powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\windows\launch_neuroseq.ps1 -NoUpdate

items.title: Developer installation
items.text: Use either uv (recommended) or Conda. You need only one of them.

items.title: Recommended setup
items.text:
Install uv and prek (a fast pre-commit), then:

uv tool install prek
git clone git@github.com:neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq
uv sync --group dev
prek install

uv sync creates .venv from pyproject.toml and uv.lock; uv run uses it without activation. Run uv sync again after pulling. To upgrade dependencies, run uv lock --upgrade, then uv sync, and test (this changes uv.lock).

items.title: Alternative setup
items.text:
git clone git@github.com:neuroseq/neuroseq.git
cd neuroseq
conda create -n neuroseq python=3.12
conda activate neuroseq
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -e . --group dev
python -m pip install prek
prek install

--group needs a recent pip. Pip ignores uv.lock and [tool.uv.sources], so package versions and PyTorch builds can differ from the uv setup. Drop uv run from the commands in these docs (for example python -m pytest).

!!! warning "uv inside Conda"

If uv is installed in an active Conda environment, `uv run` still uses the
repository's `.venv`, not Conda's Python. `conda run -n neuroseq python` and
`uv run python` can then load different packages.

Check which interpreter and versions you are using (point your IDE at the same one):

uv run python -c "import sys, brian2, numpy; print(sys.executable, brian2.__version__, numpy.__version__)"

In the embedded console, import sys; print(sys.executable) shows the running interpreter.

items.title: Everyday commands
items.text: Task Command Launch the GUI uv run neuroseq Debug logging uv run neuroseq --log-level DEBUG Run tests uv run pytest (see Testing) Run all hooks prek run -a Serve docs uv run zensical serve (see Documentation) Profile the GUI uv run python -m cProfile -o latest.prof -m neuroseq, then uvx snakeviz latest.prof

items.title: Documentation
items.text: The docs are Markdown in docs/, built with Zensical and published at https://neuroseq.github.io/. Navigation is in zensical.toml.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
Folder Content docs/getting_started/ Installation, quickstart, GUI overview, chat assistant docs/networks/ Simulators, external backends, hardware substrates docs/input_design/ Static and dynamic input design, export docs/readout/ Experiments, imported imaging and patch-clamp data docs/data_analysis/ Analyses, plugins, simulation vs. experiment docs/developer/ This guide docs/images/ Images

A new page must be added to the nav in zensical.toml.

items.title: Docs feed the chat assistant
items.text: The wheel bundles docs/ as neuroseq/docs ([tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include] in pyproject.toml). neuroseq.llm.system_prompt concatenates every .md file into the assistant's system prompt, from the installed package or, in a checkout, from the repository's docs/. Keep pages short and accurate: every word costs prompt tokens and stale text produces wrong answers.

items.title: Build and preview
items.text:
uv run zensical serve                  # live preview at the URL shown
uv run zensical build --clean --strict # what CI runs; output in site/

With Conda, install the docs group (python -m pip install --group docs) and drop uv run. prek run -a formats Markdown with prettier.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: .github/workflows/docs.yml runs the strict build on pull requests and pushes to main, and can be started manually. Pushes to main publish site/ to neuroseq/neuroseq.github.io, so the site lives at neuroseq.github.io rather than neuroseq.github.io/neuroseq. With a custom domain, that extra repository and its deploy key would not be needed.

items.title: Project undo and redo
items.text: src/neuroseq/project_history.py holds the Qt-free ProjectHistory and ProjectCommand. Each Project owns one history, shared by all its input arrays and experiments, so undo follows chronological order across them.

items.title: What is recorded
items.text:
Input value edits, generated patterns, padding and trimming, and experiment additions, appends, replacements and deletions (deleting several groups is one command). Redo reuses retained data and never repeats a file import.

These clear the history, because older commands could reference obsolete names or sample indices: creating, renaming, deleting, resampling, remapping or looping inputs, and importing project components. Simulator checkpoints, device state and console mutations are not recorded. Undo/redo is disabled while a background job runs.

items.title: Writing a command
items.text:
A ProjectCommand has a label and redo/undo callables. Use history.execute(command) to apply it, or history.record_applied(command) after the mutation already succeeded. Callbacks must:

  • validate before mutating, or roll back partial failures;
  • not hold Qt widgets;
  • raise StaleCommandError before changing anything if the target data changed outside the history (the history then drops all commands).

Experiment mutators keep array buffers by reference, so replace buffers instead of writing into them in place. Listeners refresh views; bound-method listeners are held weakly.

items.title: Lifetime
items.text: History is per project, survives saving and workspace refresh, and is not stored in .nseq files: a loaded project starts empty. Undo and redo mark the project dirty.

items.title: Making a release
items.text:
.github/workflows/release.yml publishes to PyPI when a version tag is pushed.

  1. In a pull request, bump __version__ in src/neuroseq/__init__.py and merge it into main.
  2. Once CI on main has passed, tag the merge commit with the same version (no v prefix):
git switch main
git pull
git tag 0.30.0
git push origin 0.30.0
  1. The workflow checks that the commit is on main and the tag matches __version__, builds the sdist and wheel, tests the installed wheel (including the bundled docs), uploads to PyPI and creates a GitHub release with generated notes.

Only *.*.* tags on neuroseq/neuroseq publish. The tag push does not run the test suite. Pull requests and pushes to main only build and test the package.

items.title: Publishing setup
items.text: Uploads use PyPI trusted publishing (no stored token). This needs a trusted publisher on PyPI for neuroseq/neuroseq, workflow release.yml, environment pypi, and a pypi environment in the GitHub repository settings (add required reviewers to gate uploads).

items.title: Responsible use of AI
items.text: Adapted from fastplotlib/claude-skills: Scope, Responsibility & Scientific Integrity.

items.title: Review over generation
items.text: AI tools are cheap at producing code and expensive to review. Generated code is a draft: the value of a contribution lies in the review and validation behind it. Prefer small, focused changes you can read in full over large generated ones, and do not submit code you cannot explain.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Use AI for implementation, documentation and routine coding whose expected behaviour you can check. It cannot decide whether a model, analysis or plot answers the scientific question. Without a meaningful correctness check, seek domain expertise.

items.title: Responsibility
items.text: You are responsible for every change you submit. Review it, verify assumptions and run the tests. Fluent output can hide invented APIs, changed requirements or unsupported claims.

items.title: Scientific integrity
items.text:
Code that runs and plots that look right can still misrepresent an experiment. Check against independent expectations:

  • array shapes, physical units, sampling rates and time alignment;
  • neuron identifiers across imported data, stimulus arrays and recordings; stimulation amplitudes and durations;
  • axis labels, colour scales and display limits;
  • simulation and analysis output against known cases, ideally as a scientific validation test.

Record the assumptions and validation evidence. If you cannot explain how the result was obtained and verify that it is correct, get expert review before drawing a scientific conclusion.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Tests use pytest and pytest-qt and live flat in tests/ as test_<module>.py, with fixtures in tests/conftest.py and inputs in tests/sampledata/. Every behaviour change needs a test. With a Conda install, replace uv run pytest with python -m pytest in the activated environment.

items.title: Running tests
items.text:
Task Command Full suite (up to 8 workers) uv run pytest One module uv run pytest tests/test_gui.py Serial (-s, --pdb, one test) uv run pytest -n 0 ... Coverage report uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=xml Diff coverage gate (75%) uv run diff-cover coverage.xml -c pyproject.toml Update reference screenshots uv run pytest --update-screenshot

-n auto (pytest-xdist) is the default. Tests marked @pytest.mark.screenshot are skipped unless --update-screenshot is given, which runs only them. Brian2 uses the numpy code generation target in tests. About 27 ELISE tests skip when the private elise package is not installed (see CLAUDE.md).

items.title: Writing GUI tests
items.text:
• Wait for a condition (qtbot.waitUntil, waitSignal, ...) instead of qtbot.wait(ms), and pass timeout=WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS from tests/wait_timeout.py (5 s by default; CI passes --wait-timeout=30).
  • Use waitExposed/waitActive as context managers: with qtbot.waitExposed(w): w.show().
  • Autouse fixtures silence QMessageBox and replace dialog .exec() with .show(). Use the qmessagebox_calls fixture to assert on message boxes.
  • tests/test_import_layering.py enforces the package import rules.

items.title: Scientific validation tests
items.text:
Passing unit tests do not show that a result is scientifically right. When a change affects simulation, analysis or export output, add a test that compares the scientific outcome with an independent reference: an analytic solution, a published value, or a trusted dataset. State the reference and tolerance in the test. Examples:

  • tests/test_elise_opsin_kinetics.py: integrated opsin state matches the analytic formula.
  • tests/test_membrane_parameters_analysis.py: the fit recovers the parameters of a synthetic membrane.

items.title: CI
items.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs on pull requests and pushes to main:

Job Setup conda-forge environment.yml on Linux, macOS, Windows; pytest --wait-timeout=30 --reruns 1 pypi uv, Python 3.12 and 3.14 on all three OSes; same pytest flags with coverage, then diff-cover pre-commit uvx prek run -a (ruff, mypy, prettier, nbstripout, workflow checks)

For Qt parity with CI, set QT_API=pyqt6 and PYTEST_QT_API=pyqt6.

items.title: Hardware integration
items.text:
SysCon2 tests use fake transports and need no rig:

uv run pytest tests/test_syscon2_client.py tests/test_syscon2_connection_manager.py tests/test_syscon2_panel.py tests/test_rheobase_dialog.py tests/test_stdp_window_dialog.py

On Windows, test_syscon2_client.py also opens a real named pipe to test timeouts. Pipe commands time out after 30 s (NamedPipeTransport(timeout=...)); a timeout closes the connection and does not confirm that a queued Stop arrived.

items.title: Real-rig checklist
items.text:
Run NeuroSeq and SysCon2 on the same Windows PC with the Holo4D profile (its .seq folder is C:\ProgramData\ROE\SysCon 2\2.7.2\profiles\Holo4D\Sequence Manager\Experiments\NeuroSeq) and a verified Cellpose to stim ID mapping. Check:

  1. Connect opens the pipe only; Get Status finds the light sources (940 nm preferred).
  2. Export with settings…: target power is in mW; LUT percentages are divided by 100 in .seq files (verify on the rig).
  3. Check Input Sanity resolves every violation; the timestep is exactly 520.8125 µs. Inspect the overview PNG and debug CSV.
  4. After import, the sequence appears in SysCon2 and red target crosses appear (they mark the acknowledged preview, not live illumination).
  5. Runs = 1, trigger settings, Upload, Run: progress passes through uploading, ready, starting, running; Stop during upload sends no Run. Measure timing, pattern and delivered power with the bench-test procedure.
  6. Export current array to stimulation setup reuses the last dialog settings and writes to a temporary directory.
  7. Rheobase/STDP, automatic blocks: ScanImage connected, TTL output (TargetConnectorPort) wired to the acquisition trigger. Each block's .seq, overview and sidecar are kept in the run folder, each recording .json names the right .seq, recordings start with the block, and the logged ΔF/F or spike count matches the visible response.
  8. Manual blocks: each block imported into a new, uniquely named experiment before clicking Calcium data imported; stale recordings are rejected.
  9. Routine Stop cancels only its own block; Holo4D Stop stops the hardware. Disconnect cancels communication, not stimulation.

Record the script, debug CSV, sequence, Runs, trigger, wavelength, power, frame rate, threshold and per-probe response. Still unconfirmed: the wire width of the Runs integer (sent as a 32-bit DWord).

items.title: Segfault at exit
items.text:
If tests pass and then segfault on exit inside Conda's libstdc++, preload the system runtime (Debian/Ubuntu x86-64 path):

conda run --no-capture-output -n neuroseq env LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6 QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen QT_API=pyqt6 PYTEST_QT_API=pyqt6 .venv/bin/python -m pytest

items.title: LLM Assistant (Experimental)
items.text: An optional chat panel for questions about the loaded project and NeuroSeq. It receives the documentation, a fresh project summary with each message, and read-only access to project details and the NeuroSeq source. Behaviour and supported providers may change.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
Open Settings → LLM Assistant, choose a provider and model, then click Test connection (checks sign-in without sending a prompt).

Provider Requirements Codex (local sign-in) Codex CLI and codex login. Recommended. Claude Code (local sign-in) Claude Code and claude auth login (subscription, Console account or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). Recommended. Ollama (local) (default) running Ollama daemon (default http://localhost:11434) and a pulled model (default qwen2.5:7b) OpenAI API key; any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via the base URL field Anthropic API key
  • Ollama, OpenAI and Anthropic need the chat extra: pip install "neuroseq[chat]" (installs openai, anthropic, httpx, keyring).
  • API keys are stored in the OS keyring. Without a keyring backend, NeuroSeq reads OPENAI_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
  • Codex and Claude Code: sign in under the same OS account as NeuroSeq. Leave the executable field empty to use PATH (restart NeuroSeq after changing PATH); Codex may also point to the binary bundled with its VS Code extension. Model default uses your CLI configuration; Claude Code also offers opus, sonnet, haiku, Codex lists models via Refresh.

items.title: Use
items.text:
Toggle View → Show Chat (robot icon). Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, Stop cancels. Replies stream in.

The assistant can read model equations, parameters, initial conditions, synapses, monitors, runtime state, input arrays, experiments, imaging metadata (large arrays in pages) and Python files inside the installed neuroseq package. It cannot read other files, run code or run simulations. Anything it reads is sent to the provider.

items.title: Data scope
items.text:
The Don't share project data with the provider checkbox in Settings → LLM Assistant limits what the assistant can read:

Checkbox Readable On Docs, source, model, parameters, runtime state, neuron count and duration Off All of the above, plus input arrays, experiments, Cellpose and imaging data and their names

Each provider keeps its own value. Default: on for OpenAI, Anthropic, Codex and Claude Code; off for Ollama, which runs locally. Turn it on for an Ollama server on another machine. The chat badge shows "data not shared" while it is on.

The checkbox only limits what NeuroSeq hands to the assistant. Codex keeps its own shell, file and MCP tools (it has no single switch that turns them all off), and its read-only sandbox can still read any file your user account can, including saved projects and recordings. The settings dialog warns about this when Codex is selected, and the chat badge then reads "NeuroSeq data not shared". To keep project data private, use OpenAI with an API key (or any OpenAI-compatible server, such as Azure OpenAI or a local vLLM, set as Endpoint), Claude Code (all native tools disabled) or Ollama.

Earlier replies can contain project data, so the chat clears its history (with a short note) when you switch provider or endpoint, or turn the checkbox on. Changing only the model keeps the history. Every chat panel, including detached ones and other project tabs, switches to the new settings as soon as you change them.

items.title: Writing analysis plugins
items.text:
Ask e.g. "Create an analysis plugin that plots the mean trace across selected neurons." NeuroSeq shows the target path and full code (or a diff) and saves only after you click Save plugin. Review the code: a shared project could contain text that steers the assistant towards harmful code.

  • Saved only to the per-user plugin folder (Linux: ~/.local/share/neuroseq/analysis_plugins, override with NEUROSEQ_USER_PLUGIN_DIR), never into the package.
  • Names starting with _ or matching built-in plugins are rejected; only plugins already in your folder can be overwritten.
  • Syntax is checked, correctness is not. Reopen the right-click analysis menu to load the plugin (this imports its code).

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Up to 12 read/write requests per turn; ask a follow-up to continue. Reliability depends on the model following NeuroSeq's JSON request protocol.
  • Conversations are not saved between sessions.
  • Codex runs each request in an ephemeral read-only sandbox, but your configured Codex tools still apply and its filesystem sandbox is not limited to the NeuroSeq package. Claude Code runs claude --print in an empty temporary directory with all native tools, MCP servers and settings disabled.

items.title: GUI Overview
items.text: Panels: input array editor (1), traces (2), spikes (3), synapse heatmap (4), Cell segmentation and Imaging tabs (5) and console (6). The Custom Analysis panel opens when you run an analysis. Show or hide each with View → Show … or the View toolbar (Show Data is the All data panel). Right-click a panel for Detach panel or Detach copy of panel (e.g. to compare two time windows).

items.title: Project tabs
items.text: Each project opens in its own tab (New, Open Project, an example project, or a dropped .nseq). Menus and toolbars act on the current tab. Closing a tab with unsaved changes asks to save. Only one simulation can run at a time across all tabs.

items.title: Menus
items.text: Menu Contents File New (Ctrl+N), Open example project, Open Project (Ctrl+O), Import from Project, Cell segmentation, Save Project (Ctrl+S), Save Project As..., Import data, Export, Edit Model (Ctrl+E), Generate Synthetic Data... (Ctrl+G), Manage Data Simulate Run Simulation (Ctrl+R), Store / Restore Simulation Checkpoint (Ctrl+Shift+S / Ctrl+Shift+R) Playback Set Playback Speed, Skip to Start, Stop (pause and rewind), Play / Pause (Space), Skip to End View Show panels, Toggle Selection Text, Toggle Grid, Keep Short Inputs Visible (4 px), Show all input arrays Experiment Connect (Brian2) External Input Function, Run External Input Function (external simulators) Settings See below Tools Open Fiji, Open Cellpose, Change Fiji Path… Help Documentation (F1), Source Code, About

items.title: Import and export
items.text:
Path Purpose Import data → Input → Optogenetics SysCon2 .seq (holographic stimulation) Import data → Input → Patch Clamp Igor2 .ibw/.pxp or .csv/.txt input waves (patch-clamp data) Import data → Output → Calcium Imaging (raw .tif) raw 2-photon TIFF via Cellpose + Suite2p (imaging data) Import data → Output → Calcium Imaging (Suite2p outputs) existing Suite2p results Import data → Output → Patch Clamp recorded traces Export → Patch Clamp Input input for SutterPatch (patch clamp export) Export → Optogenetic Input SysCon2 .seq files only. To also load them into a connected SysCon2, use Export with settings… in the Stimulation setup pane. Export → Traces / Spikes as NumPy Array… array of neurons × time (see below)

NumPy export: traces keep their own samples at full resolution. Spikes are counted per bin; the bin defaults to the frame period of a trace in the same data group, else 1 ms. .npy holds only the array; .npz also holds neuron_ids, times (s) and units, with the array as values.

File → Manage Data lists data groups and their data sets to rename, describe or delete them.

The file dialogs of the data imports (cell segmentation, calcium imaging, Suite2p, patch clamp, SysCon2) open in the folder that project used last, so each open project tab keeps its own folder. A project that has none yet starts in the folder used last in any project. The folder is saved with the project.

items.title: Dropping files
items.text:
Dropped files open their usual import dialog, prefilled:

File Dropped on Import .nseq anywhere project, in a new tab .seq anywhere SysCon2 sequence as an input array .ibw, .pxp, .csv, .txt input array editor patch-clamp input wave .ibw, .pxp, .csv, .txt anywhere else patch-clamp traces TIFF or PNG Cell segmentation tab cell segmentation, file ready to segment TIFF traces, spikes or All data panel calcium trace extraction TIFF, GIF or movie Imaging tab imaging data TIFF, PNG, GIF or movie anywhere else asks which of the three imaging imports

items.title: Saving and undo
items.text:
• Save Project (Ctrl+S) writes back to the current .nseq with no dialogs. Save Project As... picks a new file and which components to include. A never-saved project always goes through Save As.
  • Open and save run in the background with a cancellable progress dialog. Cancelling a save leaves the original file untouched.
  • Undo (Ctrl+Z) / Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z) cover input-array edits, imports and renames, descriptions and deletions in Manage Data. History is per tab and not saved in the file.

items.title: Data toolbar
items.text:
Comboboxes select what each panel shows: Input data, Neuron data, Spike data, Synapse data and All data (a universal panel for any traces or spikes). The button next to Input data opens array operations: create, edit, delete, clear, Trim to Mapped Neurons…, pad, trim, loop. Overlay input on traces draws the selected input array behind the Neuron data traces (each neuron's input on its own trace row) and hides the input editor. Overlay input on All data traces, next to the All data selector, does the same for the All data panel when it shows traces, for example a second calcium trace array, and leaves the input editor where it is. Each trace view, including detached panels, switches its overlay on and off on its own: right-click the traces and choose Overlay input on traces. A detached copy starts with the setting of the panel it was copied from. Every overlay follows the Input data selector and redraws after input edits, undo and redo.

The View toolbar also holds Design static input, Design dynamic input (input design), Image acquisition (ScanImage controls) and the Imaging tab's data selector.

items.title: Navigation
items.text:
• Pan: scrollbars, mouse wheel (vertical) or middle-button drag. Panels are linked by default.
  • Zoom: +/− buttons, Ctrl+wheel (time), Shift+wheel (neurons).
  • Toggle Selection Text hides the coordinate label at the cursor. The label shows the neuron and its value at the cursor time (traces: the nearest sample, with that sample's time). Times on the axis, the label and selections use seconds when 2 s or more are visible and milliseconds otherwise, with more decimals the further you zoom in.
  • Toggle Grid shows a time/neuron grid on the input editor, spaced by the array's dt.
  • Right-click the traces for Normalization… (percent scale, Center median, Clip values, Auto-extend vertical space), Overlay input on traces and Preview vector graphic…. The synapse heatmap has its own Normalization….

items.title: Comparing trace arrays
items.text:
Repeats of the same input give several trace arrays. To compare them without switching the Neuron data selector back and forth, right-click the traces and choose Compare traces…:

  • Tick any number of Neurons. The selected neuron range (or the neuron under the cursor) is ticked already. Filter the list by id or range (10-20); Select all/Select none act on the neurons the filter shows, and the field below ticks a list such as 0-5, 9.
  • Tick the Trace arrays to compare. Every trace array of the project is listed; the one the trace view shows is ticked. Drag the arrays, or use Up/Down, to set their order (it matters for Concatenated).
  • Choose a View:
  • Overlay per neuron: one row per neuron, overlaying that neuron's trace from every chosen array, each array in its own colour as named in the legend.
  • Side by side per neuron: the same rows, but every array gets its own column. The window's Side by side box switches between these two.
  • Separate window per array: one window per array, each showing the chosen neurons stacked one row per neuron. With Lock time axis (on by default), zooming or panning time in one window moves every other locked window; Lock value axis (off by default) does the same for each neuron's value range. Every window has its own lock boxes, so you can unlink a window later (ticking a box again snaps it back to the others). The windows open fanned out so they don't cover each other completely; closing one leaves the others linked.
  • Concatenated: the arrays joined end to end, in the list's order, into one long timeline per neuron. Each segment is drawn in its array's colour on its own sampling interval, starting where the previous one ended (plus the optional Gap). Dashed lines mark the boundaries and the array names label the segments.

OK opens the window(s); you can keep several open. All rows of a window share one time axis, so zooming or panning one (toolbar above the plot) moves them all. Each array is drawn on its own time axis, so arrays with a different sampling interval or length still line up in time. A neuron missing from an array is skipped there (left empty in the concatenated view), and a note at the top lists which. The windows only read the data: they change nothing in the project and add no undo step.

The one exception is Also add as new trace array to the project under Concatenated. It stores the joined traces of the ticked neurons as a new data group, named in the Name field (Concatenated: Rep 1 + Rep 2 + … by default), which then appears in the data selectors. Neurons missing from an array and the gap are filled with NaN. Adding is one undo step (Undo removes the array again). It is only offered when every ticked array has the same sampling interval; otherwise the box is disabled and its tooltip lists the arrays' intervals.

items.title: Input editor
items.text:
The left toolbar has Undo/Redo, Draw mode (1) and Select mode (2).

  • Draw mode: left-click draws, right-click erases (inverted in Erase input). Hold to draw longer. Set input value/length… sets amplitude (Constant or Ramp) and duration. Opacity shows amplitude relative to the array maximum.
  • Select mode: select all, copy, cut, paste, paste inverted, save/load region to file, delete region.
  • Show all input arrays draws the other arrays faintly behind the current one.

Details: static input.

items.title: Cell segmentation and Imaging tabs
items.text:
The Cell segmentation tab shows Cellpose cells labelled with neuron ids, each in the same colour as that neuron's traces, spikes and inputs:

  • Left click: select or deselect a cell. Traces, inputs and spikes then show only selected neurons.
  • Right drag: lasso several cells. Double-click empty space: clear selection.
  • Right click a cell: scroll the traces to its neuron (if visible).

The Imaging tab plays imported imaging movies.

items.title: Stimulation setup
items.text: View → Show Stimulation setup has one tab per target: SysCon2 (HOLO4D) (holographic stimulation), BrainScaleS-2 (BrainScaleS-2) and ScanImage (imaging) (ScanImage acquisition).

items.title: Synaptic data widget
items.text: The Heatmap panel shows the synaptic weight matrix of the selected Synapse data at the playback time. Above Settings → Synapse Matrix RAM Limit it downsamples in time.

items.title: Analysis
items.text: Select a region in the traces, right-click and pick an analysis. Results appear in the Custom Analysis panel, or in a new window if Open analysis in a new window is checked. See analysis and plugins.

items.title: Settings
items.text: Setting Effect Brian2 Simulation Backend numpy (default) or cython (simulations) Input Automatic Padding seconds of empty input added after each run (default 0) LLM Assistant provider, model, key and data scope Synapse Matrix RAM Limit MB before the synapse heatmap downsamples (default 256, 0 = no limit) Trace Plot RAM Limit same for trace plots (default 256) Theme Light, Dark or Retro light theme (beta) (default); remembered across launches

items.title: Console
items.text:
A Python console at the bottom of the window. Namespace: np, b2, plt (matplotlib) and project. Up/down arrows browse history; Console History lists it and Sample Python Code shows copyable snippets.

>>> project.stim_arrays.keys()
>>> project.stim_arrays['stimulus'].values[::10, ::2] = 1
>>> for i in range(10):
...     project.stim_arrays['stimulus'].values[i*10:(i+1)*10, i] = 1
>>> project.b2_model.monitors.keys()
>>> monitor = project.b2_model.get_monitor('trace')['object']

Direct writes to values are not undoable; use project.replace_stim_values(name, values) for an undoable edit. Read Brian2 objects but do not modify them, or the GUI gets out of sync. See help(project.b2_model).

items.title: Installation
items.text:
NeuroSeq needs Python 3.12 or newer. Install it from PyPI into its own environment.

# venv
python -m venv neuroseq-env
source neuroseq-env/bin/activate     # Linux / macOS
neuroseq-env\Scripts\activate        # Windows

# or Conda
conda create -n neuroseq python=3.12
conda activate neuroseq

python -m pip install neuroseq       # upgrade: add --upgrade
neuroseq                             # launch the GUI

The first launch is slower while dependencies build their caches. Reuse the same environment to keep them.

Further setup:

  • GPU for Cellpose and Suite2p: see Troubleshooting.
  • Working from a repository checkout: developer installation.
  • Windows desktop shortcut: Windows shortcut.
  • Optional cython Brian2 backend (Settings → Brian2 Simulation Backend, default numpy): on Windows this needs Microsoft Visual C++ 14.0 or newer, e.g. from Visual Studio 2022.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text:
1. Run neuroseq. In the Welcome to NeuroSeq dialog, click Open example project. This opens the Getting Started Project: a 10-neuron Brian2 network with an input array and a 2-photon field of view whose Cellpose cells are mapped to the neurons.
  2. Click Simulate → Run Simulation (rocket icon, Ctrl+R). The suggested duration is the length of the longest input array. Click OK.
  3. Voltage traces and spikes appear in their panels when the run finishes.

The welcome dialog also offers Load Project…, New Project and recent projects. More examples are under File → Open example project (see Examples). Next: GUI Overview.

items.title: Dynamic input
items.text: A dynamic input routine runs an experiment step by step: append one input block to the selected input array, deliver it, read the response, choose the next block. Test a routine on a Brian2 simulation, then switch its Stimulation target to run the same protocol on hardware.

items.title: Starting a routine
items.text:
1. Select the input array to extend.
  2. Click Design dynamic input (View toolbar or the editor's right-click menu), pick a routine and click Continue.
  3. Set the parameters and click Start (Start routine for STDP tuning).

If the array already holds input, choose Clear and start over or Continue after last input (hardware rheobase also offers Start in new arrays). Blocks are appended after the simulated time, never into the past, and stay in the array afterwards (undo, edit, save as usual).

One routine runs at a time: Start in another routine is refused until the running one stops. While it runs, its array stays selected and cannot be drawn on, cleared or given a pattern, and undo/redo are off.

Pause and Stop act before the next block (a running Brian2 run is not cancelled). Clear input array zeroes the array; Reset input array trims it back to the simulated time. The log records every probe and decision; live plots open in a separate window.

On a fresh model the routine first runs a short simulation to create trace monitors. If no / v trace appears, add a StateMonitor for v in File → Edit Model.

items.title: Stimulation targets
items.text:
Target Routines Amplitude means Brian2 simulation all Input array units SysCon2 (calcium imaging) rheobase, STDP window Fraction (0-1) of the export target power BrainScaleS-2 (neuromorphic) rheobase Fraction (0-1) of the tab's i_offset max

For SysCon2, Hardware settings sets power, laser, spots, recording tail (3 s), artefact removal and trace extraction (Suite2p or ROI average). With Run blocks automatically and record them with ScanImage (default) each block is run, recorded and extracted for you. Unticked, you run, record and import each block, then click Calcium data imported (rheobase) or Block done / data imported (STDP window). Use SysCon2 dt sets the array timestep to the SysCon2 grid. Details: Holographic stimulation, ScanImage acquisition, BrainScaleS-2.

items.title: Minimal input for spiking (rheobase)
items.text:
Finds the smallest input that makes one neuron spike, by bisection rather than a full grid scan. Each probe is a recovery period, a pulse, and a post-pulse window in which spikes are counted. The search tests the maximum amplitude (no spike: stop, raise it), then the minimum (spike: threshold is at or below it), then halves the bracket until it is below the tolerance or Maximum iterations (25) is reached.

Sweeping strategy:

  • Amplitude and duration: rheobase at the longest duration, then the chronaxie (duration at twice the rheobase) by bisecting duration.
  • Fixed duration, varying amplitude: threshold at one duration.
  • Fixed amplitude, varying duration: shortest spiking duration.
Parameter Brian2 SysCon2 Amplitude range / tolerance 1-100 / 0.05 0.1-1.0 / 0.05 Fixed pulse amplitude 10 0.5 Pulse duration range / tolerance 10-50 ms / 1 ms 16.7-100 ms / 1 ms Recovery time 200 ms 1000 ms Post-pulse window 20 ms 300 ms Repeats per probe 1 3

With several repeats a probe counts as a response when most trials respond. Brian2 counts crossings of Spike threshold (-20 mV). SysCon2 uses the Calcium readout: a ΔF/F rise of at least Response threshold (20 %), or OASIS-deconvolved spikes above Spike threshold (0.1 ΔF/F). BrainScaleS-2 starts with the hardware amplitudes and repeats and counts the chip neuron's spikes; connect from the dialog or the BrainScaleS-2 tab.

items.title: STDP timing window (LTP/LTD vs Δt)
items.text:
Sweeps Δt = t_post − t_pre and measures the synaptic change at each point. Use a suprathreshold amplitude (the rheobase routine can find one).

  • Readout: EPSP amplitude change (%) (five presynaptic probe pulses after each point) or Synaptic weight change (%) (reads the synapse weight directly; use it on recurrent networks).
  • Sweep mode: Reset to baseline each Δt restores a Brian2 checkpoint before every point. Continuous sweep keeps one synapse and visits Δt by increasing magnitude, alternating sign. SysCon2 is always continuous, with a calcium readout.

Defaults: amplitude 100 (0.8 on SysCon2), pulse 5 ms, Δt -100 to 100 ms in 21 points (Δt = 0 excluded), 1 pairing per point, recovery 150 ms, post-pulse window 50 ms.

items.title: STDP synaptic tuning
items.text:
Drives one synapse's EPSP to a target relative to its initial size (Brian2 only). Try it in File → Open example project → Network → Two Hodgkin-Huxley Neurons with STDP with array Exc_stimulation, trace Simulation :: P / v, presynaptic 0, postsynaptic 1.

  1. Five presynaptic probe pulses, 100 ms apart; their mean EPSP is the 100 % baseline.
  2. Outside the Tolerance window (1 %) of Target relative EPSP amplitude (120 %), append one pairing: pre before post below target, post before pre above.
  3. Probe again; repeat until within tolerance or after Maximum plasticity induction iterations (20). Run until the last iteration regardless of convergence keeps pairing.

Pairing strategy: Fixed pre-post pairing time (30 ms) uses the same interval each time. Adaptive (single parameter, dt increment) starts at 30 ms and shrinks the interval by dt increment (1 ms) when the remaining error exceeds the last EPSP change, otherwise grows it (between one sample and 1000 ms).

Pulses default to 100 (array units) for 5 ms. EPSPs are measured with the EPSP amplitudes plugin; the routine stops if the trace lacks the postsynaptic neuron or an EPSP is missed. It assumes excitatory EPSPs and pre-before-post potentiation, and timings snap to the array timestep.

items.title: Holography export
items.text: An input array becomes a .seq sequence for the HOLO4D two-photon holographic stimulation rig: one laser TTL pulse per active sample and one SLM hologram per group of co-stimulated neurons. To upload and run sequences on the rig, see Holographic stimulation.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: Item Requirement Input array dt 0.0005208125 s (520.8125 µs, one SysCon2 tick). Presets in Create/Edit input array. Cell segmentation Cellpose masks loaded (File → Cell segmentation), rows mapped to ROIs Power calibration A SysCon .lut per laser wavelength, if power control is used

items.title: Drawing input
items.text:
Each active sample is a laser TTL pulse at that tick; NeuroSeq derives the SLM holograms from the pulses.

  • Pulses can be one tick (520.8 µs) long. With spiral scanning, use at least 16.7 ms (one spiral).
  • The SLM needs one blank 16.666 ms window (32 ticks) before the first pulse to load the hologram.
  • A new hologram starts whenever the set of active neurons changes between consecutive non-empty windows. Empty gaps keep the current hologram loaded.
  • Each hologram needs one blank load window before its first pulse. With Exact stimulus timing (default) its shape starts one window before that pulse and pulses are delayed only where the previous hologram leaves no room (the first stimulus is always delayed by one window). Unticked, shapes snap to the 16.7 ms window grid, which can delay stimuli by up to one window.
  • TTL pulses keep their exact tick. Re-importing an export at the SysCon2 dt restores each pulse at the same sample.

items.title: Sanity check
items.text:
Click Check Input Sanity in the export dialog. It detects and offers to fix, directly in the input array (undoable):

  • wrong dt (Clear Array or Resample (Nearest-Neighbor)),
  • first input less than 16.66 ms from the start (Translate All Inputs Right),
  • SLM load-time gaps between neuron groups (Translate Inputs Right),
  • SLM off/on overlaps (Space Input Right),
  • neurons stimulated together with unequal durations (Equalize (to lowest value)), and overlapping pulse groups (align to the shortest),

then proposes any remaining timing or amplitude changes for confirmation. If shifted pulses no longer fit, the array is extended (with a warning) instead of cutting them off.

items.title: Export settings
items.text:
Open the export dialog with File → Export → Optogenetic Input → SysCon2 (writes files only) or Export with settings… in the SysCon2 panel (also imports into SysCon2 when connected).

Setting Default Laser timeline 940 nm digital (also 1030, 1100 nm) Target power 1 mW; 0 disables power control (intensity 0) Force binary export intensity off (amplitudes kept, clipped to 0-1) Spiralling (TTL 1 tick before SLM ready) off Exact stimulus timing on Use 10 input spots per ROI on (placement: farthest apart, or equal spacing from border) Output folder last used, first Documents\NeuroSeq\SysCon exports

Then click Generate Scripts. Files written:

File Content <name>.seq Shape and TTLPulse objects <name>_original_stim.npz The exact input array; restored on re-import. Keep it next to the .seq. <name>_overview.png Timeline overview

Power LUT. Load LUT… loads a SysCon .lut for the selected wavelength (one slot per wavelength). The requested mW is converted to the laser's intensity percentage and written as a fraction (0-1): with a linear 85 mW maximum, 5 mW is written as 0.058824. Each object's description records neuron=… power_mW=… target_mW=…. LUTs, export settings and the export folder are saved in the .nseq; save the project after loading a LUT. Use the rig's measured LUT, not a linear example.

items.title: Re-importing a sequence
items.text:
File → Import data → Input → Optogenetics rebuilds a sequence in a new or existing input array at 520.8125 µs.

  • If the _original_stim.npz sidecar is next to the file and matches it, the exact original array is restored. Otherwise timings are the hardware-adjusted ones (SLM load delays).
  • Targets map to consecutive rows from Target neuron offset, in order of first occurrence, not to project neuron IDs or Cellpose cells.
  • Replace mapped target channels clears only the receiving rows; unticked, values merge by maximum.
  • Amplitudes are raw file intensities (1 for zero-intensity shapes), not optical power. One sequence pass is imported (runs ignored).
  • Rejected: files with no stimulation, arrays over 512 MiB, objects with several timing entries or lightsources.
  • A differing dt of an existing target array is resampled after confirmation.

items.title: Input design overview
items.text:
In NeuroSeq, input is the central element. An input array streams information into a network, sets its dynamical state, and probes it (rheobase, connectivity, plasticity). The same array and the same analysis run on digital (Brian2), biological (holographic optogenetics with calcium imaging, patch clamp) and neuromorphic (BrainScaleS-2) networks. For running models and connecting devices, see Neural Networks.

Three levels, from manual to closed-loop:

Level What it does Manual input designer Draw, copy, paste and load input in the input editor, or script it in the embedded console. Static input designer Ready-made routines that generate whole patterns (sequential, simultaneous, gradient, ramp). Dynamic input designer Step-wise experiments: deliver input, read the response, choose the next input (rheobase search, STDP window, STDP synaptic tuning).

Dynamic routines can be tested on a simulation first and then routed unchanged to the microscope (SysCon2) or to BrainScaleS-2.

To run an input array on an external rig, export it with Holography export or Patch clamp export. Responses come back through Readout.

items.title: Export input for patch clamp
items.text:
File → Export → Patch Clamp Input writes input arrays for acquisition software. First choose the format:

Format Exports Igor2 - single array (.ibw / .csv) One neuron of the array shown in the editor. Set Neuron to export, Experiment name, optional unit and scaling factor. The file type follows the save dialog (.ibw by default, or .csv). Inhibitory arrays are negated. Igor2 - all arrays (.pxp) Selected input arrays as one Igor packed experiment, one wave per array. Inhibitory arrays are negated.

Export as sweeps (auto-detect period) splits a repeating column into a multi-sweep .ibw (one column per repeat); it is ignored for .csv. The scaling factor accepts forms like 1e-12 or 2.5*10^(-12).

.csv is the most portable format; .ibw imports directly into Igor Pro.

items.title: Loading a template in the amplifier software
items.text:
SutterPatch runs Sutter amplifiers inside Igor Pro. Input waveforms are built in the Routine Editor: one segment of type Template is enough.

  1. Export the neuron's waveform as .ibw (or .csv).
  2. In the Template Editor, click Import and pick the file.
  3. The template then appears in the Routine Editor's template list.

To bring recordings back, see Patch-clamp data.

items.title: Manual and static input
items.text: An input array holds one value per time step and neuron. It drives a simulation and documents what was delivered to a real sample. Drawing basics (draw/select mode, amplitude, profiles) are in the GUI Overview; this page covers the other editor tools and the static input designer.

items.title: Input arrays
items.text:
Array actions are in the Input array operations button next to the Input data selector (Data toolbar) and in the editor's right-click menu.

Action Effect Create input array Name, type (Excitatory, Inhibitory, External), number of neurons, units, timestep. Presets: SysCon2 (520.8125 µs), 1 ms, 0.1 ms, 50 µs, 30 Hz imaging. Edit input array Same fields plus duration. Changing neurons or timestep resizes or resamples the data. Delete / Clear Remove the array, or set all its values to zero (keeps its shape). Pad input array Add time to the end of all input arrays: either Seconds to add (prefilled 5 s, then the last value) or Pad to end time, the time point (s) the arrays should end at; the difference is added. An end time before the current end is refused (use Trim), and so is an amount that adds less than half a sample (nothing to pad). Trim input array Remove time from the end of all input arrays. Loop input array Repeat all input arrays end to end a chosen number of times. Clears the undo history. Trim to Mapped Neurons… Keep only neurons with a mapped Cellpose cell, in every input array and experiment. Permanent.

Settings → Input Automatic Padding sets how many seconds of empty input are added beyond the simulated time after each run (default 0).

items.title: Select mode
items.text:
Drag to select a neuron × time region, then:

Action Shortcut Effect Select all Ctrl+A Whole array. Copy / Cut Ctrl+C / X To the internal clipboard. Paste Ctrl+V Click where the region should go. Paste inverted Ctrl+Shift+V Pastes max − value, so pulses become gaps and gaps become pulses. Save to file / Load from file The selection as a NumPy .npy. A loaded array is pasted like the clipboard and must fit the array. Set amplitude to selected input Sets all non-zero samples of the selection to an amplitude you enter. Delete selected input region Delete Zeroes the selection.

Undo: Ctrl+Z, Redo: Ctrl+Shift+Z. View → Toggle Grid shows the time and neuron grid.

items.title: Scripting in the console
items.text:
View → Show Console opens a Python console with project, np, b2 and plt defined. For example:

project.stim_arrays["stimulus"].values[::10, ::2] = 1

items.title: Design static input
items.text:
Design static input (View toolbar or the editor's right-click menu) writes a generated pattern into the selected input array.

Pattern Description Sequential One neuron after another, each firing Pulses per neuron pulses. Simultaneous All neurons in scope fire together with the same magnitude. Constant Shown instead of Sequential and Simultaneous when the scope is a single neuron (see below). Linear gradient Like Simultaneous, but magnitude (and optionally pulse duration) steps from first to last pulse. Ramp A continuous linear ramp of the magnitude, repeated. Für Elise Opening notes of Für Elise on neurons 0-5 (All neurons scope only).
  • Scope: All neurons, or Specific neurons given as indices and ranges (0, 2, 5-8). Other neurons are left untouched. When the scope is a single neuron (one index, or All neurons of a one-neuron network), Sequential and Simultaneous would write the same pulses, so the two are replaced by one Constant pattern. The list updates while you type the indices; widening the scope again brings Sequential back if it was chosen.
  • Pulse duration and Inter-pulse interval (ms), or Ramp duration and Interval between ramps for Ramp.
  • Magnitude, First/Last pulse magnitude (Linear gradient) or Start/End magnitude (Ramp).
  • Pulse duration: Step from first to last pulse (Linear gradient): the pulse duration also steps linearly, from First pulse duration to Last pulse duration (ms), each rounded to whole samples. The inter-pulse interval stays the same.
  • Repeat count (named per pattern) and Start time (ms).

Apply writes the pattern and moves Start time to its end, so repeated clicks append patterns one after another. Reset start time returns to 0. The window stays open until Close.

The designer keeps its values per input array: a newly created (or newly selected) array starts from the default values, and an array you return to shows the values last entered for it, including its start time.

For closed-loop input, see Dynamic input.

items.title: Run External Simulators
items.text: An external simulator is a Python file exposing simulate(...). It receives the project's input arrays, runs its own network and returns an Experiment.

items.title: Connect and run
items.text:
1. Experiment → Connect External Input Function and choose the Python file. Use Connect Brian2 External Input Function instead if your backend builds its own Brian2 network: NeuroSeq then passes it the project's Brian2 units and code-generation target.
  2. Edit the input arrays.
  3. Experiment → Run External Input Function (or Simulate → Run Simulation, which dispatches to the connected simulator), enter the duration.
  4. Add the result as a new data group or append it to an existing one.

The connection is saved with the project. The bundled ELISE Sequence Learning Network example project comes connected to example_models/elise.py.

items.title: Data passed to the simulator
items.text:
{"stim_name": {"array": ndarray, "dt": seconds}}

The returned Experiment may hold trace, spike, synapse or other supported data.

items.title: Errors
items.text: A file that fails to load clears the connection. A failing run shows External Simulation error; typical causes are a missing entry point, a input array name the simulator expects but the project lacks, or an exception in the backend. To write a simulator, see Custom simulators.

items.title: Holographic stimulation
items.text: NeuroSeq uploads and runs .seq sequences on the HOLO4D two-photon holographic stimulation rig through SysCon2, which must run on the same Windows PC (local named pipe). Sequences come from Holography export.

items.title: Stimulation setup panel
items.text:
View → Show Stimulation setup, tab SysCon2 (HOLO4D):

  • Connection: Connect / Disconnect.
  • Sequence Manager: Export with settings…; Export current array to stimulation setup re-exports the shown array with the last settings and its own Target power box (these scripts are temporary and deleted when NeuroSeq closes). Refresh, Select, Delete the sequences in SysCon2, or Browse… and Import a local .seq into the Target directory (default neuroseq\<date>).
  • Preview: collapsed by default (Show preview).
  • Holo4D: select the imported sequence, set Runs (0 = endless, asks for confirmation), Start condition and Trigger behavior under Advanced options, then Upload (waits for Idle) and Run. The panel shows Busy/Idle and elapsed time, not percent complete. A triggered run waits until Busy is seen. Stop also cancels a queued Run.
  • Laser: read-only. Get Status discovers the lightsources (preferring 940 nm). Set power, shutter and emission in SysCon2.

items.title: Dynamic input routines on the rig
items.text:
Choose the SysCon2 (calcium imaging) target in the rheobase or STDP window dialog; Use SysCon2 dt fixes the array's timestep.

Hardware settings (SysCon2 / ScanImage) holds target power, laser, spiral scanning and 10 spots per cell (shared with the SysCon2 panel) and the recording options:

  • Run blocks automatically and record them with ScanImage (default on): each block is uploaded, run and recorded, and ΔF/F and spikes are extracted; see ScanImage acquisition. Rheobase counts a response when ΔF/F rises by the Response threshold (default 20 %) in the post-pulse window, or when OASIS finds a spike of at least the Spike threshold, depending on Calcium readout.
  • Unticked: each block is only imported into SysCon2. Run, record and import it yourself, then click Calcium data imported. Suite2p's normalised traces are refused for ΔF/F rise.

Safety limits: a block is refused without a target power above 0 mW and a LUT for the chosen laser, with a target above the LUT maximum, with amplitudes outside (0, 1], or with a stimulated neuron lacking a Cellpose ROI. Export warnings are asked once per routine.

Rheobase defaults on this target: 16.7 ms pulse (one spiral), up to 100 ms, 1 s recovery, 300 ms post-pulse window, Fixed duration, varying amplitude, 3 repeats per probe. Each target keeps its own values. With deconvolved spikes, a spike in the frame after the window still counts.

If the input array already holds input, Start offers Clear and start over, Continue after last input, or Start in new arrays (new empty array and data group named after the run, e.g. Exc_stimulation rheobase_2026-10-22_143012).

Each run saves its blocks in its own folder in the export folder, e.g. SysCon exports\rheobase_2026-10-22_143012\rheobase_2026-10-22_143012_001.seq (with PNG and sidecar), imported into SysCon2 under the same name.

items.title: Generating test data (CLI)
items.text:
# 512 × 512 image with a 10 × 10 grid of cells
neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_512.tif \
 --cellpose-grid-rows 10 --cellpose-grid-cols 10 \
 --cellpose-radius 11 --cellpose-gap 30

# 1300 × 1300 with auto-fitted radius and gap
neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_1300.tif \
 --cellpose-grid-rows 10 --cellpose-grid-cols 10 \
 --cellpose-square-size 1300

items.title: Calcium imaging acquisition
items.text:
The ScanImage (imaging) tab of the Stimulation setup pane (toolbar button Image acquisition, or View → Show Stimulation setup) controls a running ScanImage MATLAB session: Focus, record or arm a recording, abort, and grab a field of view for Cellpose. Completed recordings open in the Imaging tab. There is no live image in NeuroSeq (streaming frames slowed ScanImage down); watch ScanImage's own display.

Scope: ScanImage Premium 2023.1.0, single-plane raster imaging. Volumes, FastZ, multi-ROI and arbitrary-line scans are not supported (a configured Z-stack is fine with stacks disabled). Validate on the acquisition PC before experiments; automated tests do not prove hardware compatibility or timing.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
1. Start ScanImage with the rig configuration and, in its MATLAB window, run:
matlab.engine.shareEngine('NeuroSeqScanImage')
  1. Create a separate Python interpreter supported by that MATLAB release (e.g. 3.10 for R2023a, 3.10/3.11 for R2023b; see the MathWorks table) with the matching MATLAB Engine version, numpy and tifffile. Do not install it into NeuroSeq's own environment (Python 3.12+).
  2. In the tab, choose that Python executable, enter the session name and click Connect. NeuroSeq only attaches to an existing session; it never starts MATLAB. The Python path is remembered; the recording folder is remembered per project.
  3. Configure scanners, PMTs, channels and trigger wiring in ScanImage. Set Functional channel to the calcium indicator channel (shown in the Imaging tab and measured by routines; it must be saved). It resets to 1 each session.

NeuroSeq adds its .m files to the MATLAB path and registers its callbacks next to existing user functions (ScanImage must be idle). Disconnecting removes them; MATLAB keeps running.

items.title: Recording
items.text:
Control Default / behaviour Recording folder Each recording is one <date>_<number>.tif; Next file shows the name. Never overwrites. Experiment name Optional name of the recording's data group (else the file name) Frames 300 (routines set their own) Save channels Channel 1; tick several to save them together Wait for external acquisition trigger Off: software start. On: waits for ScanImage's configured trigger input. First-frame timeout 60 s, then abort (routine blocks use their own deadline instead)
  • Focus starts unsaved continuous imaging. Abort it before recording.
  • Record / Arm starts or arms the recording. "Waiting for first frame" does not prove the hardware is ready for a TTL.
  • Abort acquisition stops it.

For each recording NeuroSeq temporarily sets ScanImage's logging folder, file stem and counter, frames per file (unlimited), logging averaging and acquisitions per loop (1), saved channels and trigger, uses Grab (not Loop), and restores your values once ScanImage is idle after completion, abort or a failed start. A setting you change in ScanImage meanwhile is kept.

A recording completes when ScanImage reports it and the files are stable. It must contain all requested frames; an "aborted" recording that has them all counts as complete, other aborted ones are attached as aborted. The recording becomes the project's selected imaging data; the selector next to Image acquisition lists all imaging data (Import Imaging Data, Remove imaging data act on the list).

Files beside each TIFF, written before the hardware command:

  • <date>_<number>.json: request, input array (name, dt, shape, SHA-256), routine block (.seq path, SysCon2 entry) and export settings. It records the request, not proof of completion.
  • <date>_<number>_stimulus.npy: the input array samples.

The .nseq stores only metadata and a frame index; keep the TIFFs at their paths. Save imaging data… exports a rendered copy, not the original. GIF keeps recorded frame intervals; other movie formats use a constant rate.

items.title: Field of view for cell segmentation
items.text: Grab FOV for segmentation records 300 frames (software start, no stimulation), saves the mean of the Functional channel as <date>_<number>_mean.tif, and opens Cellpose on it, so masks share the recordings' pixel grid. Auto brightness (default on, remembered) stretches contrast to 0.35 % saturated pixels, like Fiji's Enhance Contrast; the same adjustment is shown in the segmentation dialog and Spatial Footprints.

items.title: Stimulation and timing
items.text: For manual runs, export, select and upload in the SysCon2 tab and arm imaging here with the external trigger. Manual recordings are marked as unverified synchronization, so planned stimulation markers are not drawn.

items.title: Dynamic input routines
items.text:
With the SysCon2 target and Run blocks automatically and record them with ScanImage, rheobase and STDP window blocks run without manual steps:

  1. Export the block, import, select and upload it in SysCon2 (1 run).
  2. Arm ScanImage to wait for the external trigger, for the block plus Record after block (default 3 s).
  3. Run the sequence (start condition auto); its TTL must trigger ScanImage.
  4. Extract ΔF/F per Cellpose ROI (F0 = mean before the block's first input) and deconvolve it with OASIS (jGCaMP8m, 0.5 s decay; events of at least Spike threshold are spikes). Options:
  5. Remove stimulation artefact (default on): frames lit by the laser are replaced by the nearest clean frames.
  6. Trace extraction: Suite2p (motion-corrected, neuropil-corrected) (default; rigid and non-rigid registration to the image the masks were drawn on, F − 0.7 × neuropil, ΔF/F relative to raw F) or ROI average (fast). Warn if Suite2p takes over (120 s) only logs a warning.
  7. Place the traces and spikes in the run's data group (e.g. rheobase_2026-10-27_153313) at the block's time.

STDP pairing blocks are not recorded. Progress appears in the toolbar progress bar and the routine's log.

Requirements and limits:

  • SysCon2 and ScanImage connected, ScanImage frame rate reported, Cellpose masks of the same FOV on the same pixel grid.
  • A recording not finished 15 s after block plus tail is aborted and the routine stops (usually a missing trigger).
  • Check the Functional channel before each run.
  • Verify the trigger wiring (SysCon2 TargetConnectorPort) and the delay from sequence start to first frame on the rig.

items.title: Interruptions
items.text: The helper is terminated if it does not answer within 30 s; MATLAB and the scanner keep running and the acquisition state is unknown, so check ScanImage before reconnecting. Closing NeuroSeq does not stop a running acquisition: use Abort acquisition first.

items.title: Rig acceptance checklist
items.text:
Verify on the acquisition PC:

  • ScanImage settings are restored after completion, abort, failed start and disconnect, and a following manual Grab uses them.
  • File names continue across restarts; frame counts and pixel values are correct, including two-channel recordings.
  • Playback orientation matches a known asymmetric target and the Cellpose masks.
  • External trigger, first-frame timeout and abort work; a routine block's TTL starts the recording and the response window lines up with the pulse.
  • Frame rate and dropped frames are the same with NeuroSeq connected (it polls status 5 times a second; each reply reports elapsed_ms).
  • Recordings survive save/reopen and attach to their own project after a project switch.

MATLAB adapter tests without a microscope (separate session, no hSI, from the repository root): assertSuccess(runtests('tests/matlab')).

items.title: Neuromorphic hardware
items.text:
