The BrainScaleS-2 tab of the Stimulation setup pane (View → Show Stimulation setup) delivers the current input array to the BrainScaleS-2 (BSS-2) accelerated neuromorphic chip and adds the response as a new data group. The chip cannot inject arbitrary currents, so input is either a constant current per segment or spikes from a virtual source population.

Verified on hxcube7fpga0chip57_1 via quiggeldy.bioai.eu:11750 (October 2026): in a 10-neuron staircase each neuron fired only during its own pulse.

items.title: How it works
items.text: The BSS-2 software (pynn_brainscales) exists only in the EBRAINS container. Connect starts resources/bss2/neuroseq_bss2_helper.py inside it with singularity exec, and NeuroSeq talks to it over JSON lines. The helper reaches the chip through quiggeldy (the BSS-2 job server). One connection is shared by all project tabs; each tab receives only its own results.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
1. Container image. Lab machines: /containers/stable/latest (default) with Container app dls. Elsewhere pull the EBRAINS image and pick the .sif with Browse… (leave the app empty):
mkdir -p tmp
SINGULARITY_TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp singularity pull \
  docker://docker-registry.ebrains.eu/esd/master/image:lab_latest.oci
  1. Setup. quiggeldy.bioai.eu ports 11717 (stable), 11750 (experimental, default) and 11780 (special). Only allow-listed IPs can connect; ask the BSS-2 team to add yours. With lab_latest only experimental worked (October 2026); the others fail with Could not submit request. Refresh also downloads the EBRAINS setup list. Host, port and expected Identifier stay editable.
  2. Token (optional). Not needed from an allow-listed IP. Otherwise paste clb_oauth.get_token() output, or set QUIGGELDY_TOKEN. The token stays in memory only, is passed through the environment, and is masked in the log.
  3. Connect. Connected chip shows the identifier (with a warning if it differs from the expected one).

Settings except the token are remembered.

items.title: Start-up time
items.text:
• Without squashfuse, each start unpacks the .sif (about 1.5 min). Build a sandbox once and select that folder instead (starts in about 1 s):
singularity build --sandbox image_lab_latest_sandbox image_lab_latest.oci.sif
  • The first activation of the container's spack environment takes about 50 s; it is then cached per image (~/.cache/neuroseq/bss2 on Linux).

items.title: Input modes
items.text:
Neurons (auto: one per input row) and Max neurons (512, one chip). Row i drives hardware neuron i; extra rows are dropped and missing ones get no input, with a warning. A single-row array drives every neuron.

Constant current (input array) (default). The array is split into segments where any row changes value. Each segment is a separate hardware run starting from rest (chained runs did not work on the chip), with

constant_current_i_offset = round(clip(value / Stim value at max, 0, 1) × Max i_offset)

and the current enabled where the value is above 0. Max i_offset: 500 (range 0-1022). Stim value at max: array maximum. Each segment costs about 0.5 s of hardware time; more than 1000 segments trigger a warning.

Spike input. A SpikeSourceArray (one source per neuron) with one-to-one excitatory synapses of Weight 63 (0-63). Spike source:

  • From input array (threshold): sample the array every Event interval (20 ms biological) and spike where it exceeds Threshold (0).
  • From project spike data: a spike dataset from a data group; neuron i drives hardware neuron i.

items.title: Time base
items.text:
BSS-2 runs about 1000x faster than biology. Speed-up (default 1000):

  • hardware ms = biological s × 1000 / speed-up (1 s of input is a 1 ms run),
  • biological s = hardware ms / 1000 × speed-up.

items.title: Delivery and readback
items.text:
Deliver current input array shows a summary and asks for confirmation. Neurons are HXNeurons with the chip's nightly calibration. The result is a data group BSS-2 <stim name> <date time> (undoable) with:

  • BSS-2 spikes of all driven neurons, and
  • BSS-2 membrane voltage (neuron n) for the neuron in Record v of neuron (one MADC, so one neuron per run), resampled to a regular step, raw units.

Stop kills the helper; a run already on the chip is discarded and you must reconnect. A running delivery keeps the project tab from closing.

items.title: Rheobase routine
items.text:
In Design dynamic input → rheobase, choose BrainScaleS-2 (neuromorphic). Connect in the dialog uses this tab's settings.

  • Each probe is delivered as constant current with the tab's settings. Probe amplitudes are fractions (0-1) of Max i_offset.
  • The probed neuron's membrane voltage is recorded. All probes go into one data group, BSS-2 rheobase <date time>, aligned with the input.
  • Every probe starts from rest; spikes after the current ends are not recorded.
  • The chip is noisy near threshold: Repeats per probe (3 on hardware targets) counts a response when most runs spike.
  • If the maximum cannot make a short pulse fire, that duration is marked (red triangle); the chronaxie search continues only if the maximum is at least twice the rheobase. Raise Max i_offset (up to 1022) for more current.
  • Stop ends the search without killing the shared helper.

items.title: Debug log
items.text: The Debug log lists every step (launch command, environment, helper versions, and with Show protocol traffic every message). The token never appears. Copy log copies it with version, host and settings for bug reports; Clear empties it.

items.title: Chip notes (October 2026)
items.text:
• pynn.run() durations are hardware ms; runs need pynn.reset() in between.
  • Constant current requires HXNeuron (not CalibHXNeuronCoba) on the nightly calibration.
  • Chained APPEND runs executed only the first part, hence one run per segment.
  • The membrane is sampled about every 32 ns hardware time (32 µs biological at 1000x).
  • Neurons differ: at i_offset 500 they fired 2-9 spikes per 100 ms pulse.

items.title: Neural Networks overview
items.text:
NeuroSeq is a neuronal sequencer: it controls the input to a neural network and reads out its output, whether the network is digital, biological or neuromorphic. For any network, input is split into controlled (what NeuroSeq delivers) and uncontrolled (everything else), and output into observed (what is recorded) and unobserved. The same input protocol and the same analysis run on every substrate.

Input arrays have one row per neuron. On biological networks, neuron ID matching links each row to a real cell through a Cellpose segmentation (File → Cell segmentation, ID Mapping Options).

items.title: Terminology
items.text:
• Import: loading files of any kind into a project. File → Import data has an Input submenu (e.g. SysCon2 .seq, patch-clamp command waveforms) and an Output submenu (calcium imaging, patch-clamp recordings).
  • Input: the arrays that drive the network, one row per neuron (input arrays, shown in the Input panel and chosen with the Input data selector). They are designed with static or dynamic input design and imported or exported as files.
  • Output: what is read out from the network: traces, spikes and synapses, simulated or recorded (selected with Neuron data, Spike data, Synapse data).
  • Stimulation: the physical delivery of input on a rig, e.g. holographic optogenetic stimulation through SysCon2, configured in the Stimulation setup pane. A stimulation artefact is laser light picked up by the imaging.

items.title: Supported substrates
items.text:
These are the integrations in use today. They are starting points for new substrates, third-party software and APIs rather than a fixed list.

Substrate Network Input Readout Digital Brian2 Input arrays drive the built-in model Simulated traces, spikes, synapses Digital External simulators Input arrays passed to your Python simulate(...) The Experiment your backend returns Biological Holographic stimulation Two-photon holographic optogenetics on HOLO4D: export .seq, upload and run through SysCon2 ScanImage calcium imaging, started or armed through its MATLAB API: ΔF/F and deconvolved spikes per Cellpose ROI Biological Patch clamp Export protocols for the acquisition software Import patch-clamp data Neuromorphic BrainScaleS-2 PyNN runs on the remote chip through a container helper: constant current per neuron, or spikes from a virtual source population; chip runs 1000x faster Spikes of all driven neurons and the membrane voltage of one neuron

items.title: Workflow
items.text:
1. Design input with the static input editor or a dynamic input routine (rheobase, STDP).
  2. Deliver it: run a simulation, export a file, or send it to a connected device from the Stimulation setup pane (View → Show Stimulation setup).
  3. Read out: the result is added to the project as a data group of traces, spikes or imaging data.
  4. Analyse and adapt. Dynamic input routines close this loop automatically on Brian2 and SysCon2 + ScanImage (rheobase also on BrainScaleS-2).

items.title: Interaction mechanisms
items.text:
How NeuroSeq talks to a network depends on what its software and hardware offer:

  • File export and import: export a protocol, run it in the other application, then import the readout. Existing protocols can be imported where the format is supported.
  • Direct API: configure and run a simulator or device through its API and get the response back.
  • Combined: generate protocol files, upload and run them through a control API, and import the recordings automatically, as with SysCon2 holographic stimulation plus ScanImage acquisition.

A file-based connection is useful on its own or as one step of an automated experiment. New backends can be added through the custom simulator interface.

items.title: Simulations
items.text:
NeuroSeq runs Brian2 spiking network simulations. The model, parameters, input arrays and recorded monitors are saved together in the .nseq project.

Action What it does Simulate → Run Simulation (Ctrl+R) Asks for a duration and continues from the last simulated time. Runs the external simulator instead if one is connected. Simulate → Store Simulation Checkpoint (Ctrl+Shift+S) Saves the network state (variables, weights, clock) under a name; pick an existing name to overwrite it. Simulate → Restore Simulation Checkpoint (Ctrl+Shift+R) Rolls the network back to a chosen checkpoint and truncates the monitors. Checkpoints are saved with the project. File → Edit Model (Ctrl+E) Parameter tree for equations, parameters, synapses and monitors. Applies on the next run.

Design the input first with the static input editor or a dynamic input routine.

items.title: Choosing a code generation backend
items.text:
Settings → Brian2 Simulation Backend:

  • cython: compiled, fastest; needs a C toolchain (see installation for Windows).
  • numpy: pure Python, always works, slower.

The backend cannot be changed while a simulation runs. For large synapse matrices see Settings → Synapse Matrix RAM Limit (GUI overview).

items.title: Experiments
items.text: Each simulation run or imported recording becomes a data group (an Experiment) holding trace, spike and synapse data. Groups appear in the Neuron data, Spike data, Synapse data and All data selectors of the Data toolbar.

items.title: Manage Data
items.text:
File → Manage Data lists every data group with its duration, description and data sets. Expand a group to see its data sets (traces, spikes, synapses) with their details (neurons, spikes, matrix size).

  • Rename (or double-click a name) renames a data group or a single data set. The new name appears in the Data toolbar selectors as group :: data set. Names must be unique (data sets: per kind within the group) and cannot contain ::.
  • Edit Description (or double-click the Description column) stores a free note on a data group, for example the slice or field of view.
  • Delete Selected removes the selected data sets only, or, for a selected group, the whole group with all its data. Input arrays are never deleted here.

Renames, descriptions and deletions are undoable (Ctrl+Z) and saved in the project file.

items.title: Generate synthetic data
items.text:
File → Generate Synthetic Data... (Ctrl+G) creates test traces for prototyping analyses. Each group has Export as a file and Add to the project; Data Preview updates as you change parameters.

Patch clamp: pick a template in Select traces, the neurons in Indexes to import, Noise (mV) (default 0.5) and Output sampling rate (Hz) (default 1000).

Imaging: fluorescence driven by a spike pattern (Select spikes).

Parameter Default Notes Recording duration (s) 10 Number of neurons 10 F0 (photoelectrons) 1000 Baseline brightness, scaled per neuron by a lognormal (mean 0, sigma 0.25). dF/F 0.4 Mean peak change for an isolated spike. dF/F variability 0.04 Indicator response Exponential decay Or Rise and decay (difference of exponentials). Rise time constant (s) 0.010 Rise and decay only; must be shorter than the decay. Not the time to peak (about 20 ms with defaults). Decay time (s) 0.050 Sampling rate (Hz) 30 Photoelectron noise factor 1.0 Shot-noise scaling.

Overlapping spike responses add up. Responses are computed at 0.1 ms and then sampled, so a sampled trace can miss the exact peak.

items.title: Segmentation test data
items.text:
To make a synthetic Cellpose image and matching segmentation from the command line:

neuroseq --generate-cellpose-test-data ./cellpose_test_grid.tif

Options are in Holographic stimulation.

items.title: Imaging data
items.text:
Calcium imaging enters a project in two parts:

  • Cell segmentation (Cellpose): which pixels belong to which cell, and which cell is which project neuron. Required for holographic stimulation.
  • Traces: fluorescence per cell, extracted from raw TIFFs or imported from Suite2p output, added as trace (and spike) data.

Patch-clamp recordings are covered in Patch-clamp data.

items.title: Cell segmentation
items.text:
Open File → Cell segmentation, or drop a TIFF or PNG on the Cell segmentation tab. A dropped file opens the same dialog with the file waiting: choose the model and Adjust brightness first as below, then click Segment file.

Segment an image: choose a Model (cpsam, cpsam_v2, cpdino, cpdino-vitb; cpsam_v2 is more sensitive on low-SNR fields) and click Select file for segmentation… with a mean-fluorescence TIFF or a PNG. Results are saved next to the image with the model in the name (fov_cpsam_seg.npy, fov_cpsam_cp_masks.png), so other models' results and a Cellpose GUI fov_seg.npy are kept. Adjust brightness first lets you set brightness/contrast before segmenting; Cellpose then segments the adjusted image.

Or load existing files: an image (PNG/TIF) and a segmentation (.npy, including Cellpose _seg.npy, or .csv). Open Cellpose and Open Fiji launch the external tools.

items.title: Neuron ID mapping
items.text:
Mapping strategy decides which Cellpose cell is which input neuron:

Strategy Mapping Linear Input neuron 0 is the cell with Cellpose ID equal to the offset, then upward; lower IDs wrap to the end. Custom Type pairs input:cellpose (e.g. 1:12,2:3), or tick Assign by clicking cells and click cells in order (unclicked cells get the remaining IDs in Cellpose order). Custom with areas of interest A square and/or circle, each preferential or exclusion. Cells in preferential areas get the lowest IDs, cells in exclusion areas the highest, each tier in Cellpose-ID order.

Input IDs are 0-based: 0 is the first input row. The SysCon2 export and the readout use the same IDs, so 1:12 always stimulates and records cell 12 as input row 1.

Area shapes can be set in pixels or percent, and dragged and resized in the viewer; the mapping updates as they move. Under Linear the shapes are shown and kept but do not change the mapping.

The segmentation is saved in the project. Delete Cellpose Data removes it.

items.title: Raw calcium imaging TIFFs
items.text:
File → Import data → Output → Calcium Imaging (raw .tif) extracts traces from one or more 2-photon TIFF stacks in the background.

  1. Add TIFF… the stack(s) and tick the ones to import.
  2. Pick Cellpose masks: those loaded in the project (with mapping), a _seg.npy file, or Suite2p auto-detection (set Cell diameter).
  3. Set the parameters and click Run pipeline.

The file list is saved with the project: when the dialog opens again, files added before are listed (unticked; files that no longer exist are dropped), so another one can be imported without browsing for it. Clear list empties it.

Several ticked files are, by default, separate recordings: each runs through the pipeline in turn (never two at once) with the same settings and becomes its own data group, named after the file (rec1, rec1 (2) if the name is taken; Simulation is reserved and :: becomes _), with its movie in the Imaging tab. The progress window names the file being processed. One summary at the end lists the imported files and the failed ones with the reason; a failed file does not stop the others. Stop after this file lets the running file finish and imports what is done; pressing it again (Abort this file too) also stops the running file. One Undo removes the whole batch, data groups and movies; Redo adds it back. Undoing a single-file import likewise removes its movie too.

The same Cellpose masks, input array and Imaging started at apply to every file, so the files must show the same field of view (frame size) and start at the same time on the input array. With Suite2p auto-detection the ROIs are found per file, and the first imported file's ROIs become the project's cell segmentation.

Choose Parts of one recording instead for a recording split over several files (e.g. ScanImage's _00001, _00002, … parts): they are joined, in list order, into one data group.

Raw stacks over ~1 GB crash Cellpose. Segment a projection instead: Open Fiji, Image → Stacks → Z Project… (Max for sparse, Mean for dense activity), save it, segment it with Open Cellpose, then load the _seg.npy. The pipeline still runs on the full stack.

Parameter Default Notes Pipeline Suite2p Or Simply average from ROI. Frame rate (fs) 30 Hz Per channel. # channels 2 1 when ROI average is chosen. Functional channel 1 Indicator tau 0.5 s jGCaMP8m. Neuropil coefficient 0.7 Spike threshold 0.02 Suite2p.

Simply average from ROI streams the stack, so long recordings (15 min at 512×512, about 14 GB) need not fit in memory. Options:

  • Neuropil correction: subtracts coefficient × an annulus of the 350 nearest pixels more than 2 px from any cell.
  • Compute ΔF/F and deconvolve spikes: ΔF/F against Suite2p's sliding maximin baseline (30 s) of the raw fluorescence; OASIS spikes counted above Spike threshold (ΔF/F) (default 0.1).
  • Stimulation artefact suppression: replaces frames lit by an input array's stimulation with the mean of the neighbouring clean frames. Imaging started at is the first frame's time on that array's axis (0 if both started together, positive if imaging started later). It is on by default only when an input array looks like pulsed light stimulation, and that array is preselected. Electrophysiology inputs (units A, pA, nA, V, mV, ...; e.g. an imported patch-clamp wave) and inputs non-zero in more than 90% of their samples are not preselected: every frame they overlap would be replaced, flattening that stretch of the traces. The import message reports how many frames were replaced.

items.title: Precomputed traces
items.text:
File → Import data → Output → Calcium Imaging (Suite2p outputs): choose the output folder (with F.npy, Fneu.npy, spks.npy, stat.npy), or pick files under Individual File Selection (.npy or .csv).

  • Traces are F − 0.7·Fneu (when Fneu is present), normalised to 0-1 per neuron.
  • Spikes come from spks.npy, kept above Spike threshold (default 0.02).
  • Max neurons to import defaults to 2; Sample rate to 30 Hz.
  • Rows are mapped to input neurons through the Cellpose mapping when one is loaded.

items.title: Imaging tab
items.text:
• Channels / Show: for interleaved multi-channel movies, set the channel count and pick the channel to play; All frames plays every frame. The TIFF pipeline presets both. ScanImage recordings use Functional channel in the ScanImage tab instead.
  • Moved files: projects store only the movie path. If it is missing, click Locate file…; other parts of a split movie are found in the same folder. Save the project to keep the new path.
  • Save imaging data…: choose frames (counted from 1; Current frame and All frames buttons), then Original frames (TIFF substack) or With stimulation marks (TIFF or GIF), which marks stimulated cells with a red "x" on a fixed grey scale.

items.title: GPU acceleration
items.text:
Cellpose and Suite2p run on PyTorch and are far faster on an NVIDIA (CUDA) or Apple Silicon (MPS) GPU. Intel integrated graphics are not supported. Check:

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"

A +cpu version or False means a CPU-only build (the Cellpose GPU option is greyed out). Install a GPU build:

uv pip install --torch-backend=auto torch

This is required on Windows, where the default wheel is CPU-only. A later uv sync can revert it; set UV_TORCH_BACKEND=auto to avoid that. In a conda environment use pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 (pick the cuXXX matching your driver). Without a supported GPU, segment on another machine and import the _seg.npy.

items.title: Readout overview
items.text:
Readout brings a network's observed output into the project as data groups (traces, spikes, synapses, imaging), matched to the same neuron IDs as the input arrays.

Page Covers Experiments Manage data groups, generate synthetic data. Imaging data Cell segmentation, neuron ID mapping, traces from raw TIFFs or precomputed outputs. Patch-clamp data Command waveforms and recordings from .ibw, .pxp, .csv and .txt files.

To analyse the data, see Data analysis.

items.title: Patch-clamp data
items.text:
Igor Pro (WaveMetrics) is the default supported software: its .ibw and .pxp files are read directly, with units, sample interval and wave notes. This covers SutterPatch, which runs inside Igor Pro. Data from other acquisition software can be imported as .csv or .txt.

Patch-clamp waveforms come in through two menu entries:

Menu Imports Into File → Import data → Input → Patch Clamp Command waveforms (input) Input arrays File → Import data → Output → Patch Clamp Recordings (voltage in current clamp, current in voltage clamp) Trace data (and spike data)

items.title: File formats
items.text:
• .ibw: Igor Binary Wave. 1-D waves, or 2-D samples × sweeps waves, whose sweeps are joined end to end (inter-sweep gaps are not kept).
  • .pxp: Igor Packed Experiment. Importable waves are listed by folder path (e.g. root/stims/HodgkinHuxley); one is selected automatically if it is the only one. Malformed records are skipped with a warning and logged.
  • .csv / .txt: comma, tab or whitespace separated; set Source sampling rate (Hz).
  • Input: one value per row, optional header with the waveform name.
  • Output: one trace per column, optional header row with unique trace names. All columns are signals (remove any time column); rows must be complete and numeric. Columns get consecutive neuron IDs from the selected one.
cell_a,cell_b
-65,-62
-64,-61

The preview shows name, format, sample count, sample interval, units, value range and Igor note. Data keep their source sample interval: no resampling on import, so different rates coexist and align by time.

items.title: Import targets
items.text:
Input dialog:

  • Create new input array: name, type (Excitatory, Inhibitory, External), units; defaults come from the wave.
  • Import into existing input array: pick array and Target neuron index. Extend target input array to fit imported duration (else overflow is cut); Replace target neuron values instead of adding to them (else values are added). Other neurons are untouched.

Output dialog:

  • Create new trace data (experiment, name, neuron ID, units) or add to existing trace data (Target neuron ID, extend, replace an existing row).
  • Detect spikes (current-clamp voltage only) stores detected spikes as spike data in the same experiment.
  • Packed experiments: import as many waves as needed, then click Close.

If the target uses a different sample interval, NeuroSeq asks:

  • Resample wave to target Δt (default): the target is unchanged.
  • Remap target to wave Δt: the whole target moves to the wave's grid. Timing can shift by one sample, and a fast recording can make the target very large.
  • Cancel.

Each import is one undoable edit.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• One wave per import, also for .pxp.
  • Sutter routine structure in packed experiments is not reconstructed, only the waves.

To export input arrays for SutterPatch, see Patch clamp export.
